utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear from you tomorrow. Do the other Defence teams have any intention to respond to the safe conduct motion? I see two times body language no intention. utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. If the court registrar can turn on the Sanction device, as that may be used during the course of the opening statement. At the Pre-Defence Conference yesterday, His Honour Judge Orie stated to the parties that when presenting their Defence case it had to focus sharply on the relevant issues in this trial, and the Defence for Ivan Cermak, in making this opening address, will present, firstly, a section concerning issues raised in the Rule 98 bis decision that are -- that are of obvious concern to the Court. The Court will then be referred to a section of evidence that the Defence contend is highly relevant and that the Prosecution had at its disposal during its case, which was exculpatory directly on the issues in this trial but did not put before the Judges. And then the Court will hear of evidence to be called from other witnesses, all present at the time, that is relevant, direct and informed and factual as to decisions that were made, which were not witnesses spoken to by the Prosecution in the preparation of their case, and, again neither were they sought as witnesses, and we say this is highly relevant material for the decision-making in relation to this case. The Court is reminded that the Defence has a right to have its evidence received in exactly the same way as the Prosecution evidence is received, with fairness and impartiality. Evidence is not the lesser because it has been produced by Defence cross-examination or because it arrives from Defence witnesses. The Defence in this case are concerned that the Prosecution has invited the Court to adopt an artificially high and unrealistic standard for criminal liability and responsibility in this case that ignores legal and factual responsibility and capabilities at the time. Expert witnesses of great experience from the Croatian system will be called. A General Feldi and Mr. Pero Kovacevic in their respective fields. Experts who will supply you with authoritative information about the military and police systems and operations within their own national system which was evidence that you were not supplied with during the Prosecution case by experts from the national system. There will also be expert international witnesses from the military. General Sir Jack Deverell from the United Kingdom, of great experience in the Balkans as a commander of NATO and of great experience in dealing with both military function, command and control, as well as real life situations where he has been on many occasions, experiencing conflict. From the police, Mr. Christopher Albiston, a United Nations police commissioner and assistant chief constable for crime of the police service of Northern Ireland. Again, great experience in this region and elsewhere throughout the world on the operating and functions of the police service. He has reviewed evidence in this case and will provide his opinion to the Court which quite clearly states that the allegations made in the indictment are unsustainable against this accused. Furthermore, also Sir Jack Deverell is of the exact same opinion. That then is the outline of our approach to the opening statement, and I will now turn to those conclusions or decisions made in the 98 bis decision. And the first concerns the issue of the personal appointment by President Tudjman of Mr. Cermak as commander of the Knin garrison. This is it found at 17.619 in the court record. The point has to be made that this appointment was totally in accordance with the law of Croatia. The Court is referred to Exhibit P1187, the Croatian Law on Service, Article 159. This was a document that was bar tabled and this Article makes it clear that the appointment to positions of the senior military are appointments made by the president. You will hear evidence from General Feldi that the appointment is totally in accordance with the law. The Court will be made aware of a mistranslation of one of the important documents on this point, which took several months to resolve, concerning how a garrison commander is designated, eventually the Defence being proved right, and the Court will be told that this position of a non-operational nature, given the background and experience of Mr. Cermak, in relation to logistics and the duties to coordinate various agencies, which he undertook at the time, were exactly what were required of him in that position. The Court will also hear as to how it came about that the post of garrison commander was selected. In relation to Mr. Cermak's duties, that of dealing with the United Nations and international groups arose as an ancillary matter to his primary appointment, which was the normalization of life. It came about as a result of the circumstances that were found to exist in Knin. This clearly indicates that Mr. Cermak was not intended, when his position was first thought of and his role in Knin considered, to be a military front man at all. But there it is. That's what happened and that has led him into this trouble. Also at that passage of the Court's decision the issue of the normalization of life and what it meant is obviously under consideration by the Court. Evidence will be heard in relation to virtually all the witnesses being called on this matter, which recite exactly the same background that this Court has heard on many occasions concerning the roles and duties of Mr. Cermak, normalizing life in Knin at that time. What is interesting is that none of those asked, none of those questioned, ascribe this as a role of law and order, which has to be the bedrock of criminal responsibility against him. Turning now to another aspect of the decision, that of meetings which took place daily at the office in Knin. The Defence will stress that it is the purpose of these meetings that is important and that the correct context be understood and accepted. They were clearly of a coordination function. Those meetings were not for the purpose of reporting crimes or other criminal events that may have taken place, and the purpose, when such facts were mentioned in those meetings, were not because he had a duty to investigate, prosecute, charge, or order. As Witness 86 made clear and the Defence witnesses confirm, the civilian police were not the subordinates of Mr. Cermak. As the Prosecution witness Buhin clearly stated, he had never met Mr. Cermak, so how a line of authority could have been in operation when that man was a coordinator with his ministry in Zagreb is open to question. The Ministry of Interior had their own line of authority by which to report and take measures. This theme is repeated throughout the Defence case, and we are anxious that the Court understands the workings of the Croatian system at that time. The fact of holding such meetings cannot create a criminal responsibility; otherwise, every person in the room, from Mr. Pasic to the man interested in electricity, would have the same liability. The Defence will have that confirmed through the witness, Mr. Albiston who quite clearly rejects that proposition as does General Sir Jack Deverell. The variety of the functions of the individuals who attended those meetings lends support to the contention that those meetings were to assist with the development and normalization of life in and around Knin. Any law and order purposes would simply not hold water in relation to the functioning of any system, and that is what we, as the Defence, are anxious in our case to ensure the Court has clear evidence. In those meetings, witnesses will confirm that everyone there was aware of the exchange and passing on of information so that people were better briefed as to what had happened and what was taking place, at all different levels of life at that time in Knin. The witness Dzolic, who gave evidence for the Prosecution, said on numerous occasions that the police were requested to do their job. Again, Defence witnesses will corroborate and confirm that theme. Everybody wanted those jobs to be done. The fact that Cermak says it does not invest within him a responsibility or authority. There has to be a foundation and basis to sustain criminal charges, and we submit our case will prove that that simply does not exist. A further passage from the 98 bis decision. Mr. Cermak's responses to crimes and his assurances that investigations would be carried out. As a proposition, the Defence are concerned about this statement. The fact that Mr. Cermak and any other person may have disagreed on some occasions as to who committed a crime or why a crime had been committed, or even whether a crime had taken place, in conversations with the international representatives, we submit, cannot, of itself, create criminal liability in this case. This would mean that communication offices for armed forces, governments, and other agencies would be liable for passing on information, which, although one party may have disagreed with what they were saying, we submit, cannot be a ground for saying that they are responsible, either for the act itself or even over the perpetrator of an act. It is tantamount to shooting the messenger. Court will hear and receive evidence which confirmed a large part of the Prosecution case that Mr. Cermak admitted crimes took place at that time. He was angry about that fact. He mentioned to many people he wanted it stopped, that he had no power himself, and his whole conduct was of a man not in denial of such events, but, in fact, of a man who wanted it stopped. Defence witnesses will testify to his intentions in relation to the Serb community, the civilians, how he wanted them to stay, encouraged factories and places of work to open, and went to the UN camp to encourage them to stay and work. This stands in great contradiction to any allegation of intent that may be put at him, which asserts he didn't want the Serbs to remain in this area. The fact that he was passing on information about crimes shows that he was not in a state of denial and intending to cover them up. The fact that he may have disagreed, however, in meetings as to what happened, why it happened, is a disagreement. It cannot be a responsibility. It cannot be a means of liability to say that he has committed a crime in relation to this indictment. The giving of assurances in relation to investigations doesn't mean that he had the power or authority to order such things. The fact that he told people that he would have something investigated showed his good intentions rather than bad intentions to those who were concerned with what was taking place. Turning now to what took place in Grubori. The Court, at 17.619 to 20, dealt in a small and brief way with how they would, at this stage of the trial, view or how the evidence was capable of being viewed, concerning what took place in Grubori. Again, a point has to be made here which is of fundamental importance. There was no eye-witness to what happened at the time in relation to the killings in Grubori and that witness was not available to state what happened. The Court knows that this was originally a report to the garrison of arson; later, two killings were mentioned. But it was someone working from the garrison itself who is a Defence witness, Lieutenant Dondo, who reported that there were five killings to the police, and we ask the Court to note that that important evidence, as Mr. Dondo will tell you, indicated that he was working in a culture at the garrison, not of concealment of crimes, but of making sure they were reported. In our submission, his evidence, which the Court will be referred to in detail later on this afternoon, is crucial on this matter. Furthermore, it became clear that this was a matter in Grubori that concerned the actions of the special police. Any person would be entitled to accept that a department of a police force would correctly and properly investigate and deal with an event with which they were concerned. It cannot be the case that we have a culture, that because the special police is mentioned in this building that anyone at that time should have suspicions or should disbelieve that they would act properly. The point we make here is that this was a matter within the Ministry of Interior from which the special police were derived, and Mr. Cermak was not in an unreasonable position in passing on any account given to him by them in explanation to the international community. There's no evidence in this case showing that Mr. Cermak knew that the version of events provided by the special police was untrue. There had only been claims made and there were no official reports alternatively put before him. The UN did not investigate this case at that time and provide an alternative forensic analysis. The danger here is that because a man believes a version and the other party has its belief of its version, that you are then held responsible for your belief or passing on what you have been told and believe to be true to others. Again, crucially, we raise this point. It is tantamount to shooting the messenger. And, again, expert witnesses will advise the Court on the systems operating in many jurisdictions relating to military spokespeople and police spokespeople who are put in the position that Mr. Cermak was at that time. The issue of freedom of movement will also be examined in the Defence case. At transcript page 17.595, the Court noted: "There is evidence that Mr. Cermak was cooperating with the other two accused with regard to freedom of movement." You will hear evidence from the liaison officers, Mr. Dondo and Mr. Lukovic, exactly how Mr. Cermak became involved in signing letters to Mr. Forand, relating to the movements of the United Nations. Crucially, these were not decisions being made by him. These were not decisions being made by him with others. These were decisions and issues that were passed through him and in respect of which he had no responsibility in the decision-making process that could hold him accountable. The fact that he passes information on to the United Nations, in our submission, does not make him liable in relation to any consequences that that may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, sorry to interrupt you. I try to follow your reference to the transcript pages. I understood you to say 17.595 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- although that's not what appears on the transcript. But 17.595 is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But nothing about freedom of movement there, because it's the first page of the 3rd of April session, which just introduces what we're going to do and that we'll first give a brief summary. So I can't follow you in your reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's in the decision, Your Honour. And I have quoted directly from it. I'm sorry, if there's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have -- oh, if you [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- reference number, I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll find it by searching for "cooperating."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 17.019. Thank you for your assistance. I try to -- whenever you make portions of the decision I try to read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I hope the Court finds that helpful. 17.619.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. Again, the fact here is that Mr. Cermak, as a conduit to be used for these decisions and to pass on notice from the Croatian authorities to the United Nations was simply being used in that form. Court will hear quite clearly from witnesses that were interviewed by the Prosecution and we will call in our Defence that he did not have that decision-making authority, and that, in our submission, is a crucial aspect for the consideration of the evidence in this case. And, lastly, on the matters within the 98 bis decision, turning to the statement in the decision, Mr. Cermak's personal involvement in securing the departure of hundreds of Serb civilians from the UN compound in Knin on buses to Serbia, the Defence, in cross-examination of Mr. Liborius, took him through a clear and long document trail on this issue, which, in our submission, clearly showed him acting as a conduit, in relation to decisions being made elsewhere on this matter. But the issue of the Serbs inside the UN camp was not exclusively a Serbian matter. There were many Croatian people inside the UN camp, and you will hear evidence from Defence witnesses confirming that fact. As days passed, people chose to leave the camp and go to their homes, encouraged by Mr. Pasic, Mr. Cermak, Dr. Dodig, a witness you will hear from, and encouraged to stay in the Knin area. As time passed, people within the camp who were Serbian decided they wanted to leave Croatia and go to Serbia. That was their decision. In a camp that was run and in place by the United Nations, Mr. Cermak was not responsible for those people going into that camp, and it became a matter between the United Nations and the Croatian government as to when and how those people within the camp would leave. The Court will be referred to a document from General Forand in which he states, You can't have your war criminals you want to investigate until we're satisfied about arrangements inside the camp for those people, if they go into Croatian custody, and, of course, we have the 800 or so Serbian people who have remained in the camp. This became a stand-off issue between the United Nations and Croatia, and largely, because, as in so many things in life, of a misunderstanding of the processes that both sides were talking about. Mr. Cermak's role, as you will hear from a Mr. Tomislav Penic, who, very soon after Operation Storm, was called in by the minister of justice and sent to Knin with files relating to suspected war criminals in that camp. When he went to Knin and saw Mr. Cermak, who took him to the camp, his view was that Mr. Cermak was more of a host for him because he and his department were dealing with this issue. All the evidence the Court has received to date has been from the United Nations side on this matter, and it's important that the Court do not have an impression, in relation to Mr. Cermak's role, that ascribes him with a level of authority he simply didn't have. Let me turn now to the next part of the opening statement which concern Defence witnesses who will be called who gave exculpatory statements to the Prosecution concerning Mr. Cermak's authority, role, and responsibility. During the Prosecution case, you heard a very narrow base of evidence on this matter. Most of it was impression evidence from international witnesses. Witnesses from the Croatian authorities were in fact very few, and of those witnesses, it has to be said, they did not agree with the proposition in the indictment that Mr. Cermak was in control of either the civil police or the military police or the military units in this area, and they rejected - Witness 86, Witness Dzolic - that they were subordinated in any way to Mr. Cermak. You heard from an expert witness, Mr. Theunens, and we will make no bones about it, we believe he presented a report tailored to suit the indictment. His evidence was based on small numbers of documents described as UNCRO orders said to prove his theory. But those documents were never actually shown to the witnesses who could have accepted or rejected the theory until cross-examined by the Defence in the course of these proceedings. So we say this has been a trial more based on theory than evidence so far, and we invite the Judges to reject speculation and consider the evidence of key witnesses who, if they had been called in the Prosecution case, we believe would have led the Court to an entirely different understanding of the nature of the case against Mr. Cermak. The Defence are now forced to call those witnesses, because witnesses have been cherry-picked, and we will produce them before the Court as well as produce the statements that they originally gave to the Prosecution. Three of these people were right in the heart of the events in the garrison. Mr. Pasic, Mr. Dondo, and Mr. Lukovic. So let's start with Mr. Petar Pasic, a Serb, a government trustee for Knin, also described as the representative or the mayor, and he was interviewed by the Prosecution in 2001, 2002. And it may be that we can even have page 4 from that statement put on Your Honours' screens, as it may assist the Court. In that statement, he stated: "I was aware that Colonel General Cermak was the commander of the Zborno Mjesto, which wasn't a Military District. As far as I know, Cermak was there to assist the civil authorities. He would direct me to organise the feeding of people which took place where Cermak had his office and he would push me to open the stores. Cermak had the logistics base and about ten or so soldiers under him. He also insisted that there be a public kitchen facility to feed the people who had no money. He wanted the civil authority to function so that he would not be bothered with the feeding of the people. Within a few days we were able to get power and water functioning in the town. "The police station was at the other end of town. I know that Cermak was appointed by the president. I did not know Cermak's area of responsibility. I would meet with him every day. There was an agenda and those items on the agenda would include, for example, an update on the power supply, how to deal with the Serbs in the UN compound, security matters. Cermak would be asking what had been done on these issues. People would respond. There were discussions about killings, looting and destruction. Often it would be Cermak who was telling us that these things were happening and asking us, asking what was being done about it. "It would have been the internationals that would have reported these crimes to Cermak and myself at a different meeting. I remember that Gambiroza would often say there were not enough policemen in Knin. My belief was that the returning Serbs or those who had remained and the internationals did not trust the Croatian police to do their job probably. Cermak would ask what had been done, and he was very unpleasant to people and would shout at them if things had not been done. As far as the killings, looting and destruction was concerned, he was not happy about it." Well, we submit there are a number of answers there in that passage to those matters raised by the Trial Chamber in the 98 bis decision which show firsthand eye-witness level what Mr. Cermak's job was, what he talked about, and what his attitude was. These are not the acts and conduct of a man embarked on a joint criminal enterprise. That doesn't fit with this description here. What's interesting about this witness as well, as the Court will see when he gives evidence, he doesn't recite a blind story about the crimes and retribution in the area at all. In fact, he condemns the authorities for those crimes and what happened and he has his own view on the matter. But what is of great significance is that he does not taint Mr. Cermak with either that responsibility or even being a supporter or sympathetic to such treatment of people in that region. Quite the opposite, as the Court will hear. Another passage at page 6, again, in contradiction to the substance of this case: "Cermak and I would go to the UN base to try and persuade the Serbs to go back to their houses. We would guarantee them safety, but others had other ideas. If they did go back to their homes, some of them were beaten, which was a message to them to stay in the UN base and not go home." Well, if Mr. Cermak was there as a member of a joint criminal enterprise, as a person showing bad intent, why would he be going to the UN camp to try and encourage people to stay? That's not this case. That's not what the Court was told in opening. That's not been the evidence that the Prosecution have tried to lead for a year. But, of course, Mr. Pasic's statement did not fit the indictment. That's why he was kept away from you. Let us go to Karolj Dondo, interviewed in 2005. A liaison officer in the region, not subordinated to Mr. Cermak, but working from the garrison, and he's been frequently mentioned in the evidence because of his role of liaison; page 3 of that statement: "Nobody joined us on the flight en route to Knin. Mr. Lukovic briefed me on what my role was to be. There was information that there was a situation at the UN camp in Knin and that Mr. Cermak was due to arrive and that we were to assist him with regard to the situation in the UN camp. The information was very brief, that there were refugees, and we should find out what the situation was when we arrived." Important to remember, Mr. Cermak wasn't responsible for anyone going to that camp. On page 4: "Our assignment was to organise the forward command of the liaison office in Knin. At the meeting with Mr. Cermak, which was very brief, Mr. Lukovic simply introduced us and explained our role. Mr. Cermak said that we were just the people he needed and that we should stay around so we were available to him. Prior to meeting him we had already moved into the Dom. I think it was the next day, on the 7th of August, that we went with Mr. Cermak to the UN camp for the first time. After that, the visits became very frequent." Page 5: "The first meeting was intended to introduce Mr. Cermak at the UN camp to General Forand. I think Mr. Cermak explained he was there to assist the UN and he was in charge of communicating with them and resolving any problems that may occur. In that sense, he was at their disposal for anything they needed. His role was also the implementation and normalization of civilian life in Knin." This is exactly what the Defence put time and time again, during the Prosecution phase of the trial, with all -- would the commander of all those units in paragraph 7 of the indictment be performing a role such as this? Assisting with regard to the situation in the UN camp? Implementing and normalizing life in Knin, resolving problems? Mr. Dondo also refers to the morning meetings, paragraph 15: "At these meetings information was passed on." And what he says is this: "At the morning meetings many people were present. Each body responsible for normalizing life would be present. There would be representatives of the civilian authorities, such as Mr. Pasic. I don't know his exact role. Representatives of the civilian police, military police. I recall that at one meeting, civil protection issues were discussed and specifically the need to clean fridges." He goes on to say: "I know that protests came in from members of the international community and our office had the role as an intermediary to pass on the information." You will hear from Mr. Dondo, and he will describe Mr. Cermak, in his view, as being a very senior liaison officer, because that was his view of what he was doing and of his role down in Knin. "So if there was a report on a house being burnt, we would pass it on. In such an example, we would pass it to General Cermak if it was addressed to him. As he was more or less the only person dealing with the UN, most of the reports were directed to him." So holding meetings where information is passed on, in our submission, was a creditable act of Mr. Cermak's, in contradiction to being an act in furtherance of a joint criminal enterprise. In fact, it shows a responsible attitude to what was happening at that time and how, as best he could, he dealt with it. Paragraph 16: "From the beginning of his time in Knin, Mr. Cermak was signing his letters and memos as the commander of the Knin garrison. According to the military regulations it is known the responsibilities of a garrison commander are for logistics and organisational affairs. So from the time that the area was liberated, Knin assumed the status of a garrison and Mr. Cermak was responsible for that area. My understanding is that he was not actually responsible for the logistics of military units in the area as they had their own logistics support. He was more concerned with the normalization of the civilian infrastructure and the logistics issues that required. As to why a military general was appointed for such a role, I can only give my own opinion and interpretation." And that was, as the Court will hear when he gives evidence, that because General Forand was a general, it would have been only right that a general from the Croatian side spoke to the general on the other side, and it was not accepted protocol for a lieutenant or captain of marine at that level to be dealing with General Forand directly. But that doesn't appear to have been put in this statement. "Because Knin was a military area at the time, and there were so many soldiers there, I think Mr. Cermak was considered to have the necessary logistical skills because of his background. As far as I know, he doesn't have the actual military rank as general, but it was more an administrative rank. From my knowledge, there is a difference between the military and administrative rank. The same thing was true when I was given the rank of captain as I was working in the rear, so while I held a rank, it was really for administrative purposes. I saw on a number of occasions that Mr. Cermak was frustrated, and I think this was because it was difficult ..." Well, again, a very clear description in non-operational terms, exactly as to how he, never having dealt with Mr. Cermak before, perceived him, and knew what his role was to be. Paragraph 17, I'll move to: "While the looting and burning was being regularly reported to him, Mr. Cermak tried to solve things. He forwarded the questions to the civilian police who were in charge of investigating such cases and then providing feedback from the police to the UN. I know that, because on one occasion, I translated the police responses on behalf of Mr. Cermak, which then went to the UN. As far as having any control over the civilian police is concerned, I can say that I never heard him issue an order to them but he would ask them to investigate and report back to him. As I saw things, he simply provided new information from the UN to the police, and as the police had no liaison officer, he was providing that role and passing on the information and asking that he was kept informed."
