utterances.text: -- not knowing what was there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I didn't know whether it would add to anything yes or no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's on a different page in my text here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 18: "I don't recall Mr. Cermak making reference to specific incidents," and he's asked this ten years later, "but there was one specific occasion, when he was returning from Sibenik, when he had seen buildings on fire. He commented that he didn't understand how or why that was happening when the Oluja operation had been over for some time. I know the media had reported that some of the burning was being done by people in military uniform, but it did not mean they were part of the military." And he goes on to explain an example that he came across exactly on that. "I am aware of what Mr. Cermak was doing to relay the complaints about looting and burning to the ranks of the military. He would pass them all to the military police and it is possible that he sent some written reports to other military structures." He recounts, in paragraph 22, on page 8, the kind of story that goes exactly to the heart of this case, and sometimes by judging what people do, you see a -- you see their clear intentions. In paragraph 2, he refers to -- 22, he refers to an incident of going to a village and a Serb was carrying water in buckets and men had slaughtered the sheep at his house. Mr. Dondo went to the house. He found four people dressed in Croatian military uniforms without insignia. Their hands were covered in the blood of lambs they had just slaughtered. They were shocked at being seen. Mr. Dondo took responsibility and talked to them. They refused to give him any information, and they said they were familiar with the area from before and knew the man. He said he was there with representatives of the UN and he noted the yard looked as though it has been put ready in preparation for being looted, and Mr. Dondo told them to stop, and he bluffed and said he knew who they were, and they then washed themselves and left. When he returned to Knin, he reported that to the civilian police, and he, despite reporting it, mentioned it to General Cermak, to see if he could do anything to help. Mr. Cermak arranged for the old man to be transferred by ambulance to the geriatric ward of the Knin hospital a day or two later. Well, in complete contradiction to the allegations in this case, and the Court will hear in some detail from Mr. Dondo, in relation to the operation required to get that man down from the mountain where he was staying and then taken to Knin hospital for treatment. Well, we say a highly significant witness who throws a complexion on the issues in this case that are direct, that are relevant, and are at the heart of it, and go to the innocence of Mr. Cermak. The third of these witnesses we'll look at in some detail will be Mr. Lukovic, interviewed by the Prosecution in 2004. He was the chief of the liaison officers, superior to Mr. Dondo, and he refers to the first meeting, as did Mr. Dondo, and he went to introduce himself to Mr. Cermak. Paragraph 34: "General Cermak told me that he had arrived Knin to help with the normalization of the town. I knew him from before but not that well. General Cermak said that he expected good cooperation from me and for me to help him with the coordination and to fully cover the liaison role. General Cermak did not explain to me his role in Knin at that meeting. It was later that I found out he was the garrison commander of Knin." But, again we get this mantra, which was our case throughout the Prosecution's phase of the trial, repeated by many witnesses about this role of normalization, a non-operational role and a role of a distinct nature that does not ascribe to it authority over units, civilian police, and military police. Let's go to page 10 and paragraph 57: "Both General Cermak and myself were very much involved in facilitating the arrangements to get the displaced persons from the UN compound who wanted to leave to be escorted to Serbia. General Cermak and I met daily with the Serbs in the UN compound. We had at least 15 meetings with them. We tried to convince the displaced persons to stay in Croatia, but it became obvious to us that there were some radicals in the compound who were telling the Serbs not to stay but to leave, and so eventually they all left. We were given a list of the displaced persons in the compound and our police did checks to identify suspects of war crimes and a small number were handed over to our police." Well, there you have it. Dondo described Mr. Cermak as a very senior liaison officer, and not expressing it in exactly those words, but the sense of what Mr. Lukovic told the Prosecution in his statement in 2004 is clearly on those lines. And what is important here is the nature of the work that he and Mr. Cermak were doing. Again, in complete contradiction to the alleged joint criminal enterprise, as described by the Prosecution in this case. And important to note with Mr. Lukovic is that he had, throughout the conflict and the war, performed this role of liaison between RSK forces and Croatian forces and involving himself with the United Nations forces, and so he was experienced in trying to broker deals and arrangements to enable the passage of life between civilians caught up in the conflict on either side and to make their lives easier. And as he describes it, he was performing what, in a sense, was more of a civilian role in that task, because he was mainly concerned with civilians, how to get food and produce from the RSK side to Croatia; wine on one occasion, something he brokered through the UN. How he was trying to make arrangements to enable people to visit families and be united. And, quite clearly, as he describes his role, that was something that Mr. Cermak, in a hands-on way took on board and he wasn't just directing or supervising, as Lukovic makes clear, he was going to the camp and expressing this. Well, to have any sense for this JCE he would have been stuck back in his office with his feet on table and just sending Mr. Lukovic down there, if that was his intent; but that's not how it was, and in our submission, goes to the truth of his role. Your Honour, that is an appropriate moment for the short adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Kay. We will have a break, and we will resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Last in this passage here but of great relevance, I'll now turn to the statement of Ivica Cetina, taken by the Prosecution in 2001, 2002. And the Court will know him as being the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration, and he describes fully the high-level police officers that were working in the Knin area and elsewhere in what we will call Sector South. It's quite clear from his statement that the police were controlling their own responsibilities, operating within their own structure, completely independently of the military and completely independently of General Cermak, who was in Knin normalizing life. Exactly the proposition that the Defence have advanced countless times over the last year. The Court will remember that during the Prosecution case the structure and systems were elucidated and put before the Trial Chamber as coherent bodies of evidence by us, showing the operation from the assistant minister of interior, Mr. Moric, down through to Zadar-Knin police administration, Kotar-Knin police administration and Knin police station through many orders, a snapshot as to how the whole thing operated and was structured. That was not evidence coming into this case through any other means other than through the means by which we presented it. He says: "As the Croatian army was liberating areas, members of the police were moving into the area and opening police stations. The ministry also assisted with logistics for newly opened police stations. There were not enough experienced Serb police officers in the Zadar police area." Court has to remember that for the previous four years, this was not an area under Croatian sovereignty, that the Croatian authorities were operating in a narrow strip of land running down the Dalmatian coast. "Therefore, appointments were made from other parts of Croatia. I personally knew all the coordinators who were sent to the liberated areas." And he describes fully all those people in the organigrams that we put before the Court, all of whom were down there on a regular basis, supervising the operation of the police. He says: "These coordinators were initially responsible to Franjo Djurica. He was the chief coordinator. After a month, he was replaced, and that coordinator, as Djurica had been, was responsible to the assistant minister for police, Mr. Moric. I was very happy with the coordinators when they were appointed, as the liberated area was huge." And the Court may have a feeling about the size and geography of this area, but the Kotar-Knin police administration area was vast, an area of much wilderness, of natural geography and an area of valleys, rivers, and areas backing up onto the mountains going towards Bosnia. As you will hear from Mr. Albiston, who's been down there, our expert police witness, a very difficult area to police. He felt it was a good move to have coordinators appointed and they knew how to deal with delicate situations. If anyone had a problem, the coordinators or commanders would communicate through him or Mr. Kardum, the chief of criminal police, but coordinators had no authority over the criminal police directly. And he says: "I did not have any special contacts with the Croatian army. The only contact I had with the military was General Ivan Cermak. I met him for the first time several days after the start of Operation Storm. To my mind, General Cermak was not a soldier in the usual sense of the word. He was more like an administrator wearing a military uniform. Although I was aware from the media that General Cermak had previously been an assistant minister of -- of economic affairs. It was my impression he was coordinating the work of the town services, ensuring electricity, water, cleaning up the town." And he recounts an occasion, again, a small incident, but capable, as with Dondo and the man in the remote area who'd had his sheep slaughtered and Mr. Cermak had him evacuated to a hospital, he also describes a very personal incident that is one many of the Court will here. He telephoned. "He told me he was at a village. I'm not sure of the location. He was there on his own initiative, and that, as the village had no power, he organised a generator, and members of international organisations were present in the village when he handed the generator to the villagers. The same evening, he called me again on the telephone and reported an incident to me. He told me that two men in a vehicle had been to the village and stolen sheep and cattle. He told me I had to do something immediately to punish the offenders. I don't remember if the generator was also stolen. I remember the police stopped the vehicle near Sinj, and that the sheep and cattle were returned to the villagers. I immediately alerted the local police commanders, and that was why the criminals were stopped." Well, why was Mr. Cermak notifying Mr. Cetina? That's obvious, because he is outside the police line of authority and control, and, on this occasion, having telephoned about the generator, was able to telephone Mr. Cetina. He said to the Prosecution in 2001: "General Cermak did not have command authority over me because I was not part of the military. My chain of command was towards the MUP central office in Zagreb and that is why I approached them." And he refers to the meetings that General Cermak had in Knin, describing them as "hosted these meetings ... they were not very formal and there was no specific agenda. We were all given the opportunity to outline our problems but no specific discussions were made. Everybody had to solve their own problems and nobody could issue an order to anybody else. These meetings were in fact only an opportunity to communicate with each other." And he goes on to say: "My impression of him was he did not want incidents like murders." Well, there we have it, in a very concise form of the relationship between General Cermak and the MUP. And in setting this before the Court, this witness, one might say, would have his own interests to serve by putting all responsibility for law and order on the military, or for the lack of it, and if General Cermak was responsible for law and order, putting it all his way, every opportunity to be self-serving, and no doubt, that was why he was interviewed. But that's not how it turned out in the interview and not what he said. And it's quite clear, when the Court were able to listen to cross-examination in the Prosecution case, the lines, the systems of the Croatian government and authorities make it quite clear where lines of responsibility are to be found. And it's our submission that, in this case, the Prosecution have failed to understand that proposition and their evidence, as one looked at the nature of the evidence called, did not seek to go down the lines of these particular statements who were all from men there at the time and part of it and gave their account. There can be no reason for not having them called by the Prosecution, having taken their statements. Enough of that. Let's move on, then, further into the Defence case, because Defence witnesses will again be called, dealing with Mr. Cermak's appointment, role and authority. How did he come to be appointed? Was he a close friend of President Tudjman, as stated in the indictment? Was there a valid reason for his role? Was he commanding police, military and running every aspect of civilian life, as asserted in the indictment? Or is that lawyer-speak in an indictment, designed to build a case rather than search for the truth, which should be the object of this trial. Did the Prosecution back up those assertions with evidence? Does the evidence called by the Prosecution so far offer a full and informed analysis of those allegations? Or is the situation going to be that, at this stage in the case, the Court, for the first time, will receive the full picture of Mr. Cermak's role, authority, and responsibility? Let's go to the president's office, then, on the day of Operation Storm, on the 4th of August, 1995. On that day, you would have seen there, in the president's office, at a place called Tuskanac, a secure facility in Zagreb near the presidential palace, but a location which was needed after the launch by Martic earlier in the year of the rockets on Zagreb, and so a facility which the president went to when Operation Storm was launched out of national safety and security. And there in the office, the Court would have seen, if it was there on that day, the man who was chief of the cabinet of the president of the Republic of Croatia, who is called Gordan Radin. And he headed the office, the secretaries, typists, the running of the office for the president. He worked under someone called Hrvoje Sarinic, who was the chief of the office of the president. And as he will tell the Court - not interviewed by the Prosecutor to pursue a line of inquiry as to how or why Mr. Cermak was appointed, a very obvious point, we would submit, to have a full picture in this case - and as he says: "After the meeting in Brioni, President Tudjman returned to Zagreb the next day, on the 2nd of August, 1995, having learned from the experience of Operation Flash. And the president issued an order and we started preparing the reserve location in Tuskanac. A small team was formed, as the president needed his work and office to function normally." And just before the beginning of Operation Storm, on the evening of the 3rd of August, the president and his team moved to Tuskanac. On the 4th of August, the president received operative reports on the progress of Operation Storm from Minister Susak. He often came to Tuskanac, and the president thought of the next steps that had to be taken. "The president asked us to find Mr. Cermak and told us roughly that he wanted Mr. Cermak as the civil commander of the town of Knin. I asked the president what that meant, and he told me that this was something like a civil commander of the town in that sense, and he wanted Mr. Cermak to come to his office. "We all tried to find Mr. Cermak, but we couldn't find him that day. We told the president that we could not find him. He insisted we find Mr. Cermak. The next day, 5th of August, we found him, and he immediately came to Tuskanac. I knew that there was a big problem to find a formal and legal way of appointing Mr. Cermak to the position of civil commander of the town of Knin because it did not exist in the government structure. We needed clarification of our task which consisted of preparing the papers. So we asked the president to explain it to us. "As far as I understood the president's explanation, Mr. Cermak was not part of the military structure, regardless of his rank. Back then, we did not have a reserve structure and everybody who was in the civil service had a certain rank. For instance, all members of the government. I, as chief secretary, had the rank of a captain. It was published in the Official Gazette. Our president was a former partisan general, and he always inclined to military ranks, orders, and he paid special attention to that fact that every country should have a certain structure ... "Since we could not find a legal basis for appointing Mr. Cermak as a civil administrator, General Kaspar called the chief of the president's military cabinet and told him to find an adequate position and way to appoint Mr. Cermak to that position as soon as possible, and to send the decision on the appointment to Tuskanac for signature. The cabinet wrote the decision on Cermak's appointment as the Knin garrison commander and sent it to President Tudjman." He goes on to say: "Cermak did not often come to the president's office. Cermak was not a close personal friend. He was not of that circle who frequently visited the president's palace and played cards and tennis with him. Mr. Cermak did not have authority to be in command of the civil police, since he was not appointed by the Ministry of the Interior." I referred the Court earlier to the exhibit which outlines appointments within the police by the minister. "The appointment of Cermak was not a kind of appointment that would give him authority to command the civil police. The military appointment of Mr. Cermak was within a regular military establishment but to the duty which enabled Mr. Cermak to take care of the civil part of obligations." And he refers to Mr. Cermak's experience previously as a minister of economy, his business experience, and that that was part of the reason why he was sent to Knin. He was a private entrepreneur who had his own business. President Tudjman was a general with a big military experience and he would not send Mr. Cermak, who had no military education, to command military units. The president wanted Mr. Cermak to cooperate with the representatives of the civil authorities, to be a mediator, to connect them and help them with one goal, to accelerate the activities from the beginning of functioning of the government institutions. And he goes on to say: "He was a civilian in uniform." There we have it then, right from the heart of the matter, where this appointment was made and answering a crucial question in this case which, in our submission, comes from a reliable source with no interest to be served, who could have been interviewed in the last ten years to find out this information. In a personal way, there's another witness called Mr. Ciro Blazevic. He was a close friend of the president, and still remaining at Tuskanac on 4th of August, he actually paid a social visit to the president that night. He did play cards and tennis with him and was someone as a friend, the president liked to have around and to talk to. And during conversation that night, he was told by the president that there would be problems in Knin, that someone needed to be appointed, to organise conditions for normal life immediately after the liberation of the town. Such a person, he said to Mr. Blazevic, would need to see problems, find solutions, a man who would enable people to return to their homes and stimulate revival. He didn't say to Mr. Blazevic that he was going to appoint Cermak, but in conversation, he mentioned that Cermak was an agile entrepreneur and had economic abilities and he was thinking of sending him to Knin. And then the next day the media published that fact and he found out through the media and put two and two together that it was Mr. Cermak who had been appointed to the role that the president was thinking about the previous evening. Let's now remain in Tuskanac and turn to the 5th of August, the day that Mr. Cermak was officially appointed and the order signed, because the Court will hear evidence of what happened, and Mr. Borislav Skegro, deputy prime minister at that time for the economy, he controlled the economic sector of the government and was responsible for finance, industry, ship building, energy, agriculture, building, and housing. He had been on holiday when Operation Storm started, but because he was deputy prime minister, he made his way to Zagreb. And on the 5th of August, at 10.00 a.m. in the morning, he was with Prime Minister Valentic, and he had heard that Knin had been liberated. President Tudjman called the prime minister and they congratulated each other over the telephone. And the president invited him to Tuskanac and so the two of them, prime minister, deputy prime minister, left the office and went to the place Tuskanac. At about noon, they met him in the shelter. There were other ministers there; Mr. Granic, Susak, Jarnjak, Radic, and others. "About ten of us. We all stood in the hall. We talked and watched the news report that a few hours earlier the Croatian army had entered Knin. It was a big historical event." President Tudjman then said: "We have to find a person we send to Knin, somebody with military experience who will revive the economy, establish communication with the UN and the international community, and who will connect the economy with military experience. Some people have recommended Ivan Cermak to me, he posed. Ivan has got experience with private business and with the army. Ivan's behaviour is not typical for a general and he will establish relations with the UN and the international community." And can you see there how moving from the 4th, when the job was first discussed, and Mr. Radin was told to look for Mr. Cermak, how it had moved on the 5th to including the component of liaising with the international community. As I said, an aspect of the job that was made ancillary to the main appointment of normalizing life. "I agreed that it was a very good choice to appoint Ivan Cermak," says Mr. Skegro. "President Tudjman sent a man who was a civilian in uniform, a businessman and former minister, and because of the international community. A message was being sent that we wanted the Serbs to remain and we encourage revival." And he goes on to give in economic terms the reason why this region was so important, why they need it, because they had a massive problem with 650.000 refugees put into the strip of coast along the seaside in Croatia and that those people would be accessing Croatian territory as an official independent state for the first time. "It was necessary to invest money in order to organise normalization of life." And he refers to the fact that the economic finances were nearly collapsing at that time and he was looking for a credit of $100 million US to prevent the collapse of the domestic currency. They knew it was necessary to urgently activate companies; for example, the Tvik company and others, that previously existed in Knin. And we have heard about this and seen this in relation to many orders and statements about what Cermak was doing. Not only does this witness establish the conversation that day relating to the appointment but provides the background that justifies it. Let us turn now to the 6th of August and move from Tuskanac down to Knin. That was the day the president visited Knin and many politicians at the same time, including Mr. Skegro. But I will take the story up from another witness, a man called Zdenko Rincic. You've heard from me about the statements of Mr. Pasic, Mr. Dondo, and Mr. Lukovic, and what they described. But Mr. Rincic arrived in Knin on the 6th of August. He was an assistant minister of economy. But he was mobilised at that time as a logistics officer for the 112th Zadar Brigade, for purposes of Operation Storm. He had known Mr. Cermak from the days when Mr. Cermak was the minister of economy in 1993. And he was present at lunch in Knin when the president was there, as well as Mr. Cermak and, indeed, other politicians, including Mr. Skegro. Mr. Rincic says this: "Later, during lunch, I managed to talk with Mr. Cermak and then he -- then told me that he was appointed as Knin garrison commander. I knew what the duties of a garrison commander were, because there was the garrison in Zadar. He is not an operative commander. A garrison commander has a duty to take care in a logistics sense of the building and infrastructure, accommodation, food of military persons, funerals of military persons. Mr. Cermak told me he had come to Knin in order to help establish normal life conditions in the infrastructural and economic area so that everyone can start working as soon as possible." He understood Mr. Cermak's job was to be the right-hand man of Mr. Pasic, whom he knew was the government's representative. "Mr. Pasic was constantly coming to Mr. Cermak's office," he said, "asking for help and he relied on Mr. Cermak for solving civil problems. I got the idea," and he means by that, on this day, the 6th, "to stay in Knin and help Mr. Cermak to restore together normal life. I phoned my minister, Mr. Vidosevic, from Zadar, where I slept," because there was no telecommunications in Knin. "I asked Minister Vidosevic permission to open a branch of the ministry of economy in Knin, and I reported the difficult situation the town was in, with no electricity, water, or telephone. Railway traffic was interrupted. And I needed support," and so Minister Vidosevic agreed. He was officially sent down there. He was given two support staff and he opened an office 200 metres away from the Knin garrison. So what happened, then, with Mr. Rincic clearly coming, as he did, from the ministry of economy. Well, of course, he went to the person responsible for normalizing life and who would make sense of his job, and that was Mr. Cermak. "We all referred to Mr. Cermak and asked for help for everything necessary for life and work in Knin." And he describes fully the meetings, who was present at the meetings, what was discussed and their purposes of coordination so that the various parts working in Knin could work in a way for the benefit of the community. Mr. Cermak's authority was clearly understood by him. "He was not superior to civil or military police. I know that the police administration and police station, in whose jurisdiction the work of civil police was, were established on the 6th of August. It was subordinated to the minister of the interior ... I know that the military police in Knin were directly subordinated to Lausic and Minister of Defence Susak. Cermak couldn't command the civil or military police. He didn't have that authority. He could only ask them to do something for him." And you will see a report, where he listed the factories that needed work and needed to be set up to get going, to benefit the community, which he sent to Mr. Cermak. And he also signed orders on behalf of Mr. Cermak, as if coming from the Zborno Mjesto, from the garrison, on tasks relating to getting the infrastructure working in Knin. And he says: "I often went to the UN camp with Mr. Cermak. We were encouraging people who worked in these factories till the liberation of Knin and who were qualified workers to leave the UN camp and return to their old jobs in the factories and remain living in Knin." And the Court will hear a protected witness still living in Knin who was one of those people who left the camp, a Serb, who had a job in a local business, and in the middle of August started working on just such one of these initiatives, inspired by Mr. Rincic, with the assistance of Mr. Cermak. And that is the summary of his evidence. Other people attending the Knin garrison at that time. Another witness, not part of Operation Oluja, who just went to Knin to help because he understood a dangerous situation concerning mines, munitions booby-traps that could have been left by the forces of the RSK, was Mr. Emin Teskeredzic, a bomb disposal expert. You've seen documents relating to him and the munitions depot in Plavno, the repeater station elsewhere in the region. You've seen him in relation to the fish farm. He is a professor of marine biology and it happened that he was down in Knin at that time, and as part of his cooperation with the garrison, in furtherance of normalization of life undertook the cleaning and restoring of the fish farm because they knew it could be a source of food for the population at that time and later in the year, and had been neglected. He describes in fact going around Knin when he was there, because a Swiss lady came to the garrison and kept on saying that Knin was heavily shelled. Because of what she said: "Her behaviour made me check personally how many buildings were damaged by shelling. I established that in the whole Knin area there were only six houses hit by shells." Something he did of his own initiative, and initiative was what was called for down in Knin at this time, and initiative as to be supplied by General Cermak to try and assist the local community. When he arrived at the garrison on the 6th of August, he understood Mr. Cermak's job from what he saw him doing, organising the reconnection of infrastructure, which was not functional, and cooperating with representatives of civil authorities. "I also saw various delegations kept coming into his office constantly, officers of UNPROFOR, and foreign and domestic delegations. "I know that Mr. Cermak had meetings in his office every day. I rarely attended. I remember that at the meetings discussions were held on what was done in respect of issues of importance for the lack of electricity, water, garbage from the city, and other jobs. "I wasn't subordinated to Mr. Cermak but we worked together. I helped anyone who needed help in relation to bomb disposal or checking the security and safety of an area." And he could see from his background in that particular branch of the military, Mr. Cermak did not command the military units in that area because it was not his task. He was not an operational commander, and the military police had their own line of command. Well, a very consistent pattern, we submit, of the nature of Mr. Cermak's role and function, further emphasised through another witness, Goran Dodig, head of the Office for Inter-Ethnic Relations of the Croatian government. He is in one of the videos we have seen, speaking outside the camp in Knin. He went to see Mr. Cermak so that he could liaise with him. Prime Minister Valentic told him to go to Knin and see what was going on there and "whether there was anything I could do in accordance with the scope of my work." "Prime Minister Valentic had told me, Mr. Cermak was in Knin and we should do everything possible. I never met Mr. Cermak before this. Mr. Cermak said he'd come to Knin to help the restoration of civilian authorities in a way that would establish normal life in the town as quickly as possible, including the quality of life. He told me he knew about me and that he knew the way I was thinking and he was pleased I had come because he lacked people." This man, in the previous years of the conflict, had spent his time attempting to negotiate between the Serbs and the Croats through international agencies and others to try and sort out differences. He is a doctor and psychologist. He, because he had met Mr. Cermak, was aware that there were problems in the camp and the conditions of life were not good for the people. So he went down to the camp as Mr. Cermak told him it might be a good idea for him to go. And when he went there, he met some of the people who had formed a council, as a form of representation to the Croatian authorities as to their needs and to create a dialogue. And so he spoke to those people, and they called themselves the Refugee Council, and he tried to organise sanitation and medical materials for them at the camp but he appreciated he had a difficult task. But on the 9th of August, he visited the UN camp with Mr. Cermak and Mr. Pasic, and that's the video that the Court has seen, Exhibit D147, and you will see him talking outside the camp, and in it he explains this was the first time he had seen Mr. Cermak at work, and he was impressed by what he was trying to do for the people in the camp. And part of the idea that they had at the meeting in the camp was that people should have passes. One has to remember that many of all of these people would not have had forms of Croatian state identification and that it was an important requirement, according to the law, and so passes were thought of as a way of giving people temporary identification papers until they obtained official personal identification documents. And that would also have been a means for people to have access to their homes, places of works, and elsewhere, and one of the reasons why those passes were introduced. Mr. Cermak left him with the impression of a man who came to do his work in a way he could and knew. Primarily, he was not a soldier. He was a man who was a good organiser, hard working. He saw problems quickly and brought solutions to try and remove the problems. And, again, this is entirely consistent with the evidence that the Defence have called -- have brought to the Court's attention in cross-examination and will continue to pursue in the Defence case. So those are some of the personnel down there in Knin at this time. We've taken it from the 4th of August, the appointment, the meetings on the 6th of August, and one gets a very clear impression, as the international military and police experts will tell you, that this is not a man working in command of police and in command of military units. It simply doesn't operate as a system like that, if this man is doing these jobs and these tasks. It's not how these structures work. Not only that. You will hear from the Croatian experts from within the system who know the system. General Feldi lectures on the Croatian military. He is responsible for writing the regulations that you have seen this in court. Mr. Kovacevic, responsible for writing the military police regulations. This Court will receive, for the first time, authoritative evidence in our Defence case, which, we submit, was sadly lacking in the previous year of this trial. Let's turn now to those who happened upon Mr. Cermak. As I said, sometimes a good way to judge what someone is thinking or doing is by how they conduct themselves, how they present themselves. Well, it so happens that the current president of Croatia, Mr. Mesic, visited Knin on a private visit, at that time, in opposition to the president, Mr. Tudjman. But he undertook a private visit to Knin to find two Serb friends who he was anxious to see again and had not seen since the split of this area from the Republic of Croatia. Well, like everyone else, he treads that well-beaten path to the door of the garrison, and he goes there because everyone knows Mr. Cermak. Some would say that was a good thing; others would say, it has been to Mr. Cermak's misfortune to be so well-known and obliging and helpful. However, President Mesic, as he now is, went to the garrison. And it was soon after Oluja. He happened to know Mr. Cermak through a mutual friend, who will also give evidence, Mr. Mladen Vedris. He was very familiar with Mr. Cermak 's personality, political views, and the kind of person he was, as he spoke to him socially and saw him on ordinary occasions. "I know that Mr. Cermak was never a person with extreme political views. He accepted all people regardless of their nationality or religious beliefs. He seemed like a businessman and a person who was capable of encouraging people within his close environment. As a former ministry of economy and entrepreneur, as well as a person with extensive life experience, Mr. Cermak was capable of organising what was necessary to restore the conditions for normal life in Knin. I could understand the reasons why he was the man who was sent at that time." So when he went to see Mr. Cermak, what was Mr. Cermak concerned with? Was he commanding all those hordes of units in paragraph 7 of the indictment, as this case has been presented? Was he controlling any form of military at all from that garrison? Or was it just as it was on the bottle, so to speak? It was a place where steps were taken to bring a normal life to Knin. Well, let's see what he saw. "While I was in Knin I met Ivan Cermak. He sincerely welcomed me and we had lunch in the office. During lunch we had a discussion about the work he was doing in Knin. He told me about the efforts needed to restore all the public services in the town and what he was doing in order to restore normal life for people in Knin." And he explains the problems about how this area had been cut off from the sovereignty of the state and many institutions were not present. No institutions were present, there was no connectivity of this area within the mainstream of its mother state, and in our submission, that's a picture that is very necessary to emphasise in this case as to what the problem was in the area that had been newly liberated and which the president here puts in a very clear way. "There were no shops, banks post offices." Nothing was connected to the mainstream of life. "I remember our lunch was interrupted at least ten times by people who addressed Mr. Cermak and asked for information about electricity, water, transport of rubbish, the opening of a bakery shop, and other important issues concerning public services. During all that time I spent with Mr. Cermak, he neither talked about military matters nor were such matters mentioned. I was under the impression that his work was entirely civilian in nature." He visited Knin again, next time in September, as part of an official visit with the assistant commissioner of the Croatian government for Knin. Nothing had changed on that second visit as to what Mr. Cermak was doing and what they discussed and the problems that he raised with them, and they raised with him. So there, the small, spontaneous cameo picture that we submit goes right to the heart and gives the answer to this case in a very clear and positive way as to what Mr. Cermak was doing. You've heard so far within this address some of the very positive steps taken to help people who were in trouble and with problems. Further evidence abounds within the Defence relating to that kind of conduct by him which is the drawing together on a personal level of what he did, as well as on a factual and legal level, as to what he was doing. You will hear from a witness called Nadan Vidosevic, who at that time was ministry of economy under Mr. Skegro, deputy prime minister who was at Tuskanac on 5 August when Mr. Cermak was appointed, and this man was the minister who approved that Mr. Rincic, who worked with the garrison and was an assistant minister of economy, went and stayed in Knin and worked with Mr. Cermak. He explains very clearly, as you would expect from his role, the problem that Croatia was facing in economic logistic terms with this particular region. 650.000 refugees were displaced persons, accommodated along the Croatian coast-line. That was 15 percent of the Croatian population living outside of their homes. One-third of all refugees were people from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Republic of Croatia was a devastated country, as he describes it, in 1995. And he was keen to enable Mr. Rincic to work with Mr. Cermak and knew exactly what they were trying to do down there in this region. So this appointment and job of his is not some fanciful alternative the Defence have produced to try and explain a man's conduct and what he was doing at the time. It's actually based on fact evidence, documents, as well as utterly reliable people of responsibility who are keen to assist this Court get to the truth. You will hear, again, from another witness, Mr. Vedris, a spontaneous source of evidence in the same form as President Mesic. He was a -- the colleague and business partner, whom -- for a period, whom Mr. Cermak and Mr. Mesic knew separately. But they were linked together and developed their contact and friendship of each other. But he had an office in Zagreb in the same building as Mr. Cermak. And in August 1995, Mr. Cermak, on occasion, had to leave Knin to go and attend to his private and personal affairs. You will hear he just suddenly had to leave his business, which still had to run. It still had to have its decisions taken. There still had to be accounts prepared, and that required him to return to the office. Again, to assist the Court as to what they talked about and what was on Mr. Cermak's mind as an indicator of what he was doing, this has been included for reasons of how spontaneous it is in the same way as President Mesic. When Mr. Cermak was coming back from Knin, he had these conversations and they were linked to three points. First, it was the communal issue to restore life; secondly, he had contacts with international institutions; and, thirdly, he was trying to get resources of certain ministries going so their sectors could start working in Knin. And he knew, because he had been the mayor of Zagreb, what it took to run a city. He had also been a person within the political world who had been approached to become prime minister on previous occasions. So a man of great experience. And what they were talking about was the civil side of life, because that was Mr. Cermak's job. And he was talking with him, because of his experience as mayor, that it was going to be very difficult, under the conditions, for Mr. Cermak to get the government and institutions involved. Cermak replied he wanted help and was trying to activate the government, and explaining to them what was going on in Knin, and he wanted to raise the level of awareness in Zagreb about what was happening in Knin. "He told me he felt frustrated because of these crimes and because he could not adequately replay to the UN questions about the crimes." So there we are. That is part of this section of evidence that we hope will inform the Court. So what went wrong? Why do we have this issue in the case that has not really been examined in any great detail in the course of the Prosecution as to why, on numerous occasions, people have said this was not a planned military series of operations or conduct or a deliberate military policy to drive these people from their homes by committing crimes? Why do we have this issue of the civilians being responsible? Why do we have this issue as to it being a natural and spontaneous revenge by those who had earlier suffered? Because that's what was said on many occasions to those UN interrogators in 1995 and what is the explanation given by many of the parties who were present and involved in those events. Well, why? And we will be providing the Court evidence through the 92 bis evidence system of other trials in this building, relating to crimes committed in the period from 1991 to 1995 by the Serb population in this area against the Croatian population. And the Court will hear, will be able to read, no doubt it will be summarised at some stage, about the destruction, burning, looting, destruction of religious cultural monuments, torture, shelling, and killing of civilians to drive them out of the area. This problem was not, in our submission, looked at or considered in any detail in the Prosecution case. But that picture given by Minister Vidosevic of 650.000 people down on that coast-line, all waiting to get back to their homes, who've heard the stories of what had been happening since 1991, who had experienced themselves what had happened, who had had relatives who experienced what had happened, in our submission, provide the basis for the reasonable inference that the assertions made by Mr. Cermak and others at the time, that civilians bent on revenge were largely responsible is not unreasonable. Virtually every single one of these witnesses will be able to give you their own story of speaking to someone who wanted to take it out on someone else, from senior people to ordinary people. Mr. Skegro tells quite pointedly the account of speaking to a neighbour on an island who had spent his whole time saying what he was going to do to those who driven from his home and burnt down his family home. And as he said, I couldn't reason with him. We don't know whether he did, but that -- that was the frame of mind, and this aspect of the case, we submit, is essential and needs to be explained and brought to life so that the Court can see that these expressions are not unreasonable views. The UN or internationals may have disagreed, but to disagree doesn't make you responsible in some way, because you don't hold the same point of view. There were clear grounds to justify those statements made by Mr. Cermak and others. Not that they were exclusively blaming civilians. He said some military units may be involved, some police. Others would say the same. It's not an attempt to provide a whole blanket of explanation and be blind to the truth. But what we say here is that the grounds for what happened have not been properly looked at and will certainly be, as all three Defence cases emerge in this trial in the remaining time, an explanation of what happened. And in the last part of my presentation to the Court, there will be a section of witnesses for whom protective measures are to be sought, so I will not refer to them by name. They're from Knin, and they give their account as to how they came to the camp when Operation Oluja started, and people took shelter. None of them state that -- that Knin was devastated or bombed out of recognition. They all say that there was slight bombing and slight damage near military or government installations. The most that they saw amongst them were two or three places that were damaged. Teskeredzic, as I told you, counted six when he went around the town. And all of them will tell you how they came to get to the UN camp, and that was at a time when they were taking shelter with others in basements, and the talk amongst everybody was about going to Serbia, the planned evacuation. That was -- that was on the mind of everybody, that there was to be a planned evacuation. And, in fact, as one witness will tell you, the RSK forces were telling people when to leave their shelter, and they decided to remain and not leave. In fact, one of those witnesses was in the same shelter as Martic. Interestingly enough, the planned exodus of people to Serbia, when they knew that the days of the RSK were up, happened. These people stayed behind. They got to the camp when they emerged on the 5th from their various and distinct basements and they came across Croatian forces. They all gathered, on the 5th, at various points and they were told that it would be better off for their safety if they went to the UN camp. And so transport was arranged. So no issue of being removed from the area, taken out, but for reasons of personal safety, quite understandable, the Court may think, in the circumstances of where there has been a conflict and a war, that that is a reasonable place for people to take shelter. What are the risks if the army had left them to remain at large? Well, they could get damaged in any activity if any RSK forces remained there and were fighting with the Croatian forces. There was no certainty of outcome, and all military operations have to be carefully planned and to take into account contingencies. So all these witnesses went to that camp for their safety and they did not think that that was unreasonable. And when they went to the camp, they were aware of a distinct contingent of people, advising others to go to Serbia, because they knew the option was remaining either in Croatia or going to Serbia. Many people took the Serbian option. These decided to stay. They got their passes. They went out of the camp to their homes, and they went and started working, and -- in their various places, which I will not describe because of the request for protective measures. And, again, there you have it. This is the end product of that line of normalization of life where people are being looked at to open factories, get back to their warehouses, get to their hospital and start treating people. This was the end product of why General Cermak had been sent down to Knin and why he was coordinating and liaising with those people out of the garrison. We submit that this is very important evidence. Again, it -- it contradicts the concept of the joint criminal enterprise, and, again, I'm going to refer to one more witness who has a cameo story which contradicts the JCE. He has made three statements to the OTP, the Prosecution, in which he described how people in his area where he lived in Plavno were killed by some Croatian forces. So three statements on that matter. And that witness, then, one could take it, as a Serb giving those statements, would be no lover of anyone in Croatian authority. But he tells, again, another of those accounts which go to show what General Cermak was doing. In mid-August, Croatian police came to his door and asked whether he and his wife had registered and whether they had identification passes. They hadn't, so they went to Knin. And they went to the garrison. And there, they introduced themselves and spoke to soldiers. They were told, General Cermak's been looking for you. And so this elderly gentleman, now in his 80s, went to see General Cermak. That time in his late 70s. And the first thing that General Cermak said, How are you, young man? Sit down. I'm looking for you because I have been contacted by your family and they're anxious that you and your wife -- to find out if they are well. And that was it. So for an hour he spoke with General Cermak, told him about his circumstances. This man had his arm broken by the RSK forces just before the 4th of August, when they were getting people to leave the area, and so he had to go to hospital. So what did General Cermak do with this gentleman? He arranged that food was delivered every week from Knin to this remote area of Plavno so that he and his neighbours were provided with food and the necessities of life. A touching story. He will tell you as well that when he heard General Cermak was being taken to The Hague, he went to the newspapers to complain and said, I will go to The Hague to speak on his behalf. And, fortunately he was traced and if he is well enough and fit enough, we should be able to get him here. Otherwise, we invite the Court to listen to him by videolink. A very touching story. And as we say, undercuts entirely the substance and intentions behind this Prosecution because that is the truth of the matter, that's what General Cermak was doing on a daily basis, not this joint criminal enterprise, as described by the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honours. That is the finish of my opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. I'm looking at the clock and I'm wondering, Mr. Mikulicic, whether you would prefer to start today. We'll hear no witnesses tomorrow. So whether you would like to -- because you had asked for the number of hours we could not complete today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- we have the time. So I leave it your hands whether you'd like to do it in one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be preferring the position of my opening statement to be not restricted by time today so that I can going up from tomorrow morning in a contents, I mean, not it disrupt the statement. I would prefer that situation but, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- it is up to Your Honour to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will not lose anything if we would allow you to give your whole opening statement tomorrow. I will just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the total of time you would need was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That means an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hour and a half. Yes. Then of course you could not start, if we could continue today, any earlier than ten minutes past 6.00 which would leave you 50 minutes. Then it would -- I do agree with that you it's more -- it's better for you and better for the Court to hear it not interrupted by 12 hours. If you would need, you said one session. If you would not be able to finish it in one session, at least we would have only a break of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 25 minutes rather than having to catch up tomorrow morning on what you started today. Therefore, we will allow to you start tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One little question, Mr. Kay, for my part. I know most of the words that are spoken in this courtroom but the word "cameo" is not -- I'm not entirely familiar with, and under those circumstances, I tried to use some resources but to say that that helps me very much, no. Could you explain to us what you meant by a "cameo story," for example. I think you used the word twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and it was for a particular reason. Cameo role you hear of as a little picture, and so in a drama or a play someone has a cameo role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- like the grave diggers in Hamlet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I understood how you use this word. I'D rather ask what I do not know, Mr. Kay. One other thing came to my mind when listening to you, and I'm actually also looking in the direction of the Prosecution. You spoke about a lot of things where we'll hear evidence on and what your concerns are in the 98 bis decision. There is, however, one area where I wondered to what extent there is big dispute about, and that's what happened between 1991 and 1995, where you said, The events may explain what has happened. Now, I do understand that the parties will not easily agree on whether this explains what happened. But what happened from 1991 to 1995, of course, you could argue about whether there were 625 refugees or whether there were 585.000 -- 625.000 or 585.000 refugees, and whether it was a small area at the Dalmatian coast or whether it was a bit wider. But I wondered to what extent the parties could agree or compromise on, I would say, the main body. Not to say that not -- no evidence should be presented, but for the way of presenting the evidence it might well be that further discussions between the parties would make it possible to, at least from a factual point of view, to know about the events which you say may explain what happened. And even if the Prosecution would not agree with that, whether that explains what happened, whether it caused civilians to do all kind of things. You could perhaps agree on what had happened during those years. Or, if not in full, to find out where there is some common ground and that additional details, where you disagree, that then, of course, the Cermak Defence would present its evidence. That is a thought that came into my mind, and I would invite, Mr. Waespi, the Prosecution, to seriously think about it, and if it gives any opening to explore possibilities, because, as always, matters that are not really in dispute should be mentioned, should be presented, but can sometimes be presented in such a way that it takes less time in court without affecting in any way the information the Chamber receives. We will adjourn for the day. We will resume tomorrow, the 29th of May, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.
